output.brief: The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not a location effect. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20.0% vs 21.1%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2%, close to the 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and job mix doesn't explain it. Caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real gap of a few points can't be ruled out. Manager comments hint at informal favouritism in who gets urgent work, but that isn't measured. Don't confirm proximity bias or announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Instead, pause it, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, track stretch-work allocation, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Confidence: fairly high.
